claims.statement: CEFR Pre-A1 describes a narrow early speaking profile built largely from short phrases, words and formulaic expressions, including simple personal information and highly bounded interaction; it does not require broad generative conversation as the entry criterion.

When productive ability is an instructional goal, production-based practice contributes to productive learning and can show a relative delayed advantage over comprehension-only practice, so comprehension success should not be assumed to become speaking skill automatically.

Low-proficiency adult EFL learners can benefit from output-based preparation before speaking; in one large controlled study, productive planning through writing improved speaking scores and fluency relative to reading model answers.

Pre-task planning changes subsequent oral performance, with effects differing across complexity, accuracy, lexical complexity and fluency depending on planning implementation and task conditions; planning provenance therefore matters when interpreting speaking evidence.

For novice L2 learners, task complexity and the type of guided planning can create different fluency/accuracy/complexity trade-offs; vocabulary-guided planning can reduce production burden while complexity increases can create dysfluency or accuracy costs.

Repeating oral tasks can improve dimensions of oral performance, but gains depend on task/repetition conditions and same-task repetition is practice on a trained episode rather than evidence of spontaneous transfer to an unseen speaking task.

Standardized interactive speech tasks can elicit and distinguish interactional subskills such as meaning negotiation and repair with useful rating reliability, supporting bounded scripted interlocutor tasks as a diagnostic option before fully open conversation.

Oral corrective feedback supports L2 development in classroom evidence, and prompts that require self-repair can be particularly useful; however, current evidence does not establish one universal automated feedback sequence for every target and learner.

Formulaic sequences are legitimate instructional units that can support L2 performance, while the evidence does not establish a universal near-A0 chunk inventory or prove that formulaic production alone demonstrates broad generative speaking ability.

Repetition, reading aloud, model-visible production, independent short production and contingent interaction impose different response demands; speaking claims must therefore be tied to the elicitation task and support visible at response time.

RQ-006 does not establish the validity of automatic speech-recognition scores, pronunciation scores or one global fluency metric as measures of near-A0 speaking proficiency; those decisions remain dependent on pronunciation and ASR validation.

The exact speaking-task unlock thresholds, planning/support fade, repetition dose and transition from bounded interaction to open conversation for Vietnamese-speaking near-A0 Nếp learners are not established by the literature and require product experiments.
